params.prompt: Selling to Dennis and Gloria draws extra scrutiny. Maryland’s Medicare supplement rules require advertising to be filed with the Insurance Commissioner before use and prohibit cold lead devices, which are mailings that hide their insurance purpose, high-pressure tactics, and any suggestion of government endorsement. Twisting, misrepresentation and the use of titles implying Medicare expertise beyond a producer license are banned. Producers must make reasonable efforts to determine that a policy is appropriate: it may not duplicate Medicare, an Advantage plan or another supplement, and it may not be sold to someone on Medicaid except in narrow cases. Excessive insurance is itself a violation.

At application the producer delivers the federal buyer’s guide, Choosing a Medigap Policy, and an outline of coverage that summarizes benefits and premiums in a standard format. Maryland gives the applicant thirty days after delivery to return the policy for a full refund, and that right must appear prominently on the first page. If the sale replaces another supplement, a replacement notice is signed, the application asks about existing coverage, and the new insurer must credit the time already served under the old policy, waiving pre-existing condition, waiting, elimination and probationary periods for benefits the old policy covered.

A Maryland supplement must provide at least the federally required minimum benefits, and its deductible and coinsurance benefits must change automatically when Medicare changes, so Dennis never finds a gap opened by a January adjustment. A policy may not duplicate benefits Medicare already pays, may not use exclusions or limitations stricter than Medicare’s, and may not be offered at an unapproved introductory rate. It may not be canceled or nonrenewed except for nonpayment or material misrepresentation, and a spouse’s coverage may not end merely because the insured’s coverage ends. If the insured becomes eligible for Medicaid, benefits and premiums are suspended for up to twenty-four months at the insured’s request.

A Maryland supplement may exclude a pre-existing condition for no more than six months, and may define one no more strictly than a condition for which a physician gave advice or treatment in the six months before coverage. Prior creditable coverage reduces the wait, and replacement eliminates it for covered benefits. Compensation rules protect buyers from churning: a producer’s first-year commission may not exceed two hundred percent of the renewal commission, renewal commissions must continue for a set number of years, and a replacement sale earns only the renewal rate, so there is no bonus for moving Gloria from one supplement to another.

Beyond the federal six-month open enrollment at sixty-five, Maryland adds protections. People under sixty-five who qualify for Medicare because of disability must be offered Plans A and D for six months after Part B enrollment, and the Plan A premium may not exceed the average paid by policyholders sixty-five and older. Since July one, two thousand twenty-three, Maryland has a birthday rule: for thirty days after each birthday, an existing policyholder may switch to a policy with equal or lesser benefits from any insurer without underwriting, and insurers must give notice of that right thirty to sixty days before the birthday. Group supplements that end must offer individual conversion, and continuation applies when membership ends.

Medicare Select is a Medigap policy with a network. For full benefits the insured must use the plan’s network hospitals and sometimes physicians, except in emergencies, in exchange for a lower premium. Benefits are otherwise the standard lettered plan. A Select policyholder has the right to switch to the insurer’s standard version of the same or a lesser plan without underwriting if she moves out of the network area or at any time during a stated window. Theo explains to Gloria that Select saves money only if her hospital is in the network, and that the Maryland rules in this lesson apply to Select as fully as to any supplement.

Dennis keeps his job at a sixty-employee firm after turning sixty-five. Under the Medicare secondary payer rules, when an active employee or spouse age sixty-five or older is covered by a group plan of an employer with twenty or more employees, the group plan pays first and Medicare pays second. If the employer has fewer than twenty employees, Medicare pays first and the group plan second. Retiree coverage is always secondary to Medicare. Because his employer is large, Dennis may delay Part B without penalty and enroll during the eight-month special enrollment period after he retires.

Two more rules. A person under sixty-five who has Medicare because of disability and is covered by a group plan of an employer with one hundred or more employees, through her own or a family member’s current employment, has the group plan primary and Medicare secondary; under one hundred, Medicare pays first. For end-stage renal disease, the group plan is primary for a thirty-month coordination period beginning with Medicare eligibility, regardless of employer size, after which Medicare becomes primary. Employers may not offer incentives to drop group coverage in favor of Medicare or treat Medicare-eligible employees differently.

Medicaid is the joint federal and state program that pays for health care for people with limited income and resources. In Maryland it is called Medical Assistance and administered by the Department of Health, with federal rules and matching funds. Since the Affordable Care Act expansion, adults with household income up to one hundred thirty-eight percent of the poverty level qualify on income alone; children, pregnant women and parents have higher thresholds, and the Maryland Children’s Health Program covers children in moderate-income families. Eligibility for long-term care coverage adds a resource test with a low asset limit and a five-year look-back on transfers of assets.

Medicaid covers mandatory benefits in every state: inpatient and outpatient hospital care, physician services, laboratory and x-ray, nursing facility care, home health, family planning, transportation to care and comprehensive screening and treatment for children. Maryland adds optional benefits including prescription drugs, dental for adults and home and community-based services that help people stay out of nursing homes. Medicaid is the payer of last resort: every other coverage pays first. People eligible for both Medicare and Medicaid are dual eligibles, and Medicaid or a Medicare Savings Program may pay their Medicare premiums and cost sharing.

Gloria assumes Medicare will pay if she needs a nursing home. It will not, beyond a narrow window. Medicare covers skilled nursing care for up to one hundred days after a three-day hospital stay, with coinsurance after day twenty, and skilled home health care on an intermittent basis. It pays nothing for custodial care, the help with bathing, dressing and eating that most long stays require. Medical insurance and Medicare supplements exclude custodial care as well. Medicaid does pay for custodial nursing home care, but only after Gloria spends down her assets to the eligibility limit. Long-term care insurance is the private product designed for exactly this gap.

Dennis, sixty-six and working for a large employer, has his group plan primary and Medicare secondary; when he retires, Medicare becomes primary and a supplement fills the gaps. His brother, disabled at fifty-eight and covered through a spouse’s five hundred-employee company, has the group plan primary. Gloria, seventy-one and on Medicare, has Part A for a hospital stay and one hundred days of skilled rehabilitation, but a year of custodial care would fall to her savings and then to Medicaid, unless she holds a long-term care policy. Lesson forty-seven builds that policy, and Lesson forty-eight adds Maryland’s rules for it.
